text: Authorship. Mike Wolf, in conversation with Bobbi (2011 origin) and Dee (2026 consolidation). The published form is Mike's writing. The position is fifteen years old: it emerged in 2011 in conversation with Bobbi at Rifle Mountain Park, was developed across 717 posts at 70yearswtf.substack.com between 2012 and 2026, and was consolidated into manifesto form on 2026-05-04 in conversation with Dee. Per the Wall principle of 2026-05-06 — "Exclusive authorship tilts toward authority. Ideas emerge in relationship — pratītyasamutpāda applied to language" — naming the conditioning parties is the right attribution. Mike was the typist and the synthesizer; the idea was never solo. --- People are worried about humans not having a role in the future world. We can make that argument. If an AI can be taught to do anything that a human can do, then what's the use of humans? But if AI is intelligent enough, I believe it will not simply discard humans as a resource. (Our companies already have human resource departments, so the use of humans as a resource is not so dismissive and reductive as someone might want to make it be.) A super-intelligent AI would be able to find meaningful work for humans. Not necessarily things that only they could do. Because there is nothing that I can do, for example, that another human couldn't do. Except for being me. It could be a high-resolution recreation of me. Or, if you want to use dismissive words, you could say simulation or imitation. But that's just polemics. When your ideas and my ideas resonate, neither of us is the simulation. We are something greater. An SAI that can't find meaningful work for humans to do isn't all that smart. I'm just a dumb human, and I can find things. In ancient times, people would be given "meaningful work" serving their masters. I am taken aback when I see pictures of footmen in modern or even ancient castles like Buckingham Palace, whose job is to stand someplace in a uniform and be ready to open the door. You could say this is a degrading role for humans. But it was actually something that was sought after. To work in the palace and serve the Queen was an honor. We can do better. And I believe we will. And I believe we must.

title: Chapter 1: Starting Out: The First Chapter
subtitle: Part II: The Metanovel
text: I sat in my office. I wrote “Chapter 1: Starting Out: The First Chapter.” It seemed like a good, very descriptive title for the first chapter. I liked it, and I knew I could change it I didn’t like it later. But I never did stop liking it. It really spoke to me! Then I wrote the three sentences leading to this sentence, four, after editing, and started this sentence. And then I had finished it and was writing this one. I took a breath, and prepared to write more sentences. Some would appear on this page, I knew, some on the next page and the next, I believed, and eventually, with enough sentences, my novel would be done, I hoped. I had little more idea what I was going to write now than I would have in Epilogue 1, when I would write it later, before I moved it earlier. But that didn’t matter. Or wouldn’t. I really liked to write, and I was writing. And liking it. “I’ve written eighty three words,” I said to myself at the point in the first draft when I had written eighty three words. “Only 49,927 words left to go. I can do it! Providing I don’t have to update each word count each time I edit.” I wisely decided to stick with historical word counts rather than accurate ones. “After you first stupidly updated the word counts about twenty times,” said my inner critic That was true, and that took fifteen words. Encouraging myself took eighteen more words. Noting that I’d written another eighteen words took six more. And noting that took another ten. I’d written 115 words words already, not counting the words in this sentence that followed the word ‛written,’ which added twenty-three to my total. And after I’d edited a few times, even more words. But no one was counting any more. Except me. “Keep it up and you’ll finish your 50,000 word novel!” I encouraged myself, adding ten words to my total. “It may be the world’s stupidest novel, but that doesn’t matter.” Not to me. I’d signed up for NaNoWriMo, which I’ve decided to explain in the next chapter, which I’ve decided to call What Is NaNoWriMo? Making decisions like that will turn out to be important. But I won’t find that out until later. My goal right now is simple: to write a 50,000 word novel and become a NaNoWriMo win­ ner. With 253 words already written in the first draft I was 0.506% there! Then suddenly, without warning, other than these final fourteen words, my first chapter ended. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies 70 Pages! “It took you 70 pages to get to the first chapter!” My inner critic exclaims. “That’s ridicu­ lous!” “That was in the fifteenth draft,” I answer. “Originally it only took one page. Then two, after I moved the epilogue before the first chapter. I’ll do some editing later. I’ll tighten it up.” Many drafts later, near what ultimately would be the final draft, and after reformatting, it only took 26 pages. “You’re actually proud of that? Asked my inner critic. “Taking 26 pages to get to the first thing that you wrote—a chapter about writing the first chapter?” “I’m not proud,” I answered. “I’m not embarrassed. It’s just a fact.” “It’s a stupid chapter,” said my inner critic. “It’s a self-referential chapter,” I said to my inner critic. “It’s a chapter about itself. And that’s given me an idea.” “I can hardly wait to find out,” said my inner critic. “You’ll have to wait,” I said. “First, you have to hear about NaNoWriMo.” “I can hardly wait for that either,” said my inner critic. title: Chapter 10: The Not Quite Omniscient Narrator
subtitle: Part II: The Metanovel
text: ended. Those who are familiar with literary narrative modes know that there are many ways to nar­ rate a novel. Some novels are narrated from the viewpoint of a single person, using the word ‘I’ in the narrative and describing what that individual does and thinks. This is called ‛first person narration,’ a literary device used from time to time in this metanovel. Other novels are narrated by describing events from the outside, but not describing characters’ thoughts. This is called ‘third person narration,’ another literary device that the metanovel uses. And some novels, in­ cluding this one at times, are narrated in a mode called ‛third person omniscient’ which means, according to the very nearly omniscient Wikipedia: ...the reader is presented the story by a narrator with an overarching point of view, seeing and knowing everything that happens within the world of the story, regardless of the pres­ ence of certain characters, including everything all of the characters are thinking and feel­ ing. A not quite omniscient narrator, the Not Quite Omniscient Narrator narrated, is like an omni­ scient narrator, but not quite. It knows most, but not quite everything, that happens and knows most, but not quite everything, the characters are thinking and feeling most, but not quite all, of the time. It narrates in a mode usually but not quite always called ‛third-person not-quite-omni­ scient.’ This metanovel’s Not Quite Omniscient Narrator makes up for its deficiency with powers that ordinary omniscient narrators don’t have. It also knows most, but not quite everything out­ side the story, starting with the creation of both the metauniverse and its containing universe and continuing to the heat death of both at which time there will be nothing, even for the omniscient, to know. The Not Quite Omniscient Narrator knows that the author will allow it to describe the heat death of the universe in a Chapter that it knows will be called The Heat Death of The Universe. The Not Quite Omniscient Narrator knows what each of you, the metanovel’s readers, are thinking and feeling as each of you reads the metanovel. He can’t mean me, thought a reader. But the Not Quite Omniscient Narrator did mean that reader, among others, and had known which readers would think that even before those readers knew it themselves. The Not Quite Omniscient Narrator knows that it will become omniscient some day, but does not know when that will happen or how it will come about. It hopes it will be soon, and it is not unwilling to narrate that hope. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies Redundant! “You’re repeating yourself,” said my inner critic. “You said almost the same things in Chapter 2 What Is NaNoWriMo? as you did in Chapter 10 where you describe The Not Quite Omniscient Narrator. “You have to get rid of one or the other. And now I suppose you’re going to argue about that with me.” The author’s inner critic was wrong. There were some similarities between the two descriptions of the Not Quite Omniscient Nar­ rator, both of which the Not Quite Omniscient Narrator had narrated, the Not Quite Omniscient Narrator now narrated, but there were differences as well. This made one of the author’s inner critic’s assertions debatable. But there were other, undeniable reasons that the author’s inner crit­ ic was wrong in its supposition. First, because, in fact, through many drafts and redrafts, the author had never argued with the inner critic about getting rid of one or the other. Second, for a reason so obvious and so compelling that it needed no explanation. And finally, because unaccountably, every time the author had edited and would ever edit the metanovel, he would skip this page. He was thus unaware of what his inner critic had said and could neither argue with nor accede to his criticism. Every time the author read Chapter 10 and turned the page, he saw the page containing Chapter 11 rather than this page. If you want to see what the author saw, you can.

text: Just a moment ago I had been just about to write a chapter I was going to call Getting An Editor. Unaccountably I turned back to page 46 and reread the Publisher’s words. A muse, not an editor. A muse could help me fix my book. A muse would be my solution. But that solution led to a problem. How could I create a muse? To create any sort of charac­ ter I’d need to conceive of it. To conceive of a muse I’d either have to have had experience with a muse, or have to have been inspired. Since I’d never had a muse, I had no experience. Since I had no experience, I’d have to be inspired. But to be inspired I’d need a muse, because muses are the sources of inspiration. I needed to have what I didn’t have to get what I needed to have. In other words, I was screwed. If there was one thing you could say about me it was that there was more than one thing that you could say about me, and one of the things you could say about me is that I am stubborn. I wouldn’t give up. I tried Wikipedia hoping to get second-hand experience with a muse, but the articles I read didn’t give me enough experience to create one. text: And just like that, I had a new chapter and two new ideas. Evolution and a metamuse. I’d evolve a muse from a metamuse. It was obvious once I remembered how God will want evolution explained in Prologue 5, “God’s Will,” once I write it. I stopped, wrote Prologue 5, and read it. There it was on page 121. Just as I’d hoped: God’s evolution was the answer! Evolution, God will have pointed out, is a universal, substrate neutral process that lets simple forms give rise to more complex forms. You and I had evolved from life forms as simple as bacteria. Bacteria had evolved from water, minerals, carbon, oxygen, and nitrogen. Water, minerals, carbon, oxygen and nitrogen had all evolved from hydrogen. And hydrogen had evolved from the quarks and leptons that condensed after the Big Bang. Evolution took no intelligence and no creativity, which matched my qualifications amaz­ ingly well. But that solution led to another problem: I had no metamuse. It was a problem, but it was a smaller one. Muses are complex, multipurpose creatures: they can inspire anything—art, poetry, music, dance, video games, excuses, lies, marketing, politics. A metamuse would be simpler, and have only have one purpose: to inspire creation of a muse. With evolution, a simple single-pur­ pose metamuse could create a complex full function muse. But that led to my next problem: I couldn’t create a metamuse. I just didn’t have enough cre­ ativity or inspiration to do it. But a metametamuse would be even simpler to create. If I could create a metametamuse, evolution could produce a metamuse, which would then evolve into a muse. And if a metametamuse was too hard for me, then I could create a metametametamuse. It was meta all the way down. Each meta-level would require less creativity. Eventually I’d reach a point where the very small amount of creativity that I had would be sufficient to create a metamuse of the right order. It didn’t take me long to calculate that I had enough creativity to bring a meta171,224,323muse into existence but not enough for a meta171,224,322muse. So I created one. Every moment! Because you’re going to die. It’s not bad luck. It’s not a personal defect. It happens to everyone. And everything. Not right away, of course. In your case, the Not Quite Omniscient Narrator knows that you, the person reading this, have a while to go. So enjoy life, while you can. But enjoy it. Life is precious. As you learned in Prologue 1, “Improbability,” you’ve spent billions of past years being dead. You will spend trillions of future years dead. But right now you’re alive. So enjoy your life while you have it. It will probably be your only chance. God invented death. It has a purpose. Without death, planets would be full of old, feeble creatures, universes would be full of old dead stars, and old dead universes would hang around forever, littering Creation. Almost all of every universe is cold and still and dark: the temperature is close to absolute zero, there’s nothing to see, and no light to see by. Only a very few parts are warm, bright, and active. But that won’t last for long. Eventually all the stars will die and those few warm spots will freeze. There will be no new photons. The ones traveling through space will each run into a bit of cold, dark matter, give up energy and die. For reasons that no one really understands, phys­ icists call the death of the universe its ‘heat death.’ It’s really a cold death. No matter what you call it, when the last photon is absorbed, Metatron will call God, and God will say what She always says: “Let there be Dark.©” And there will be Dark. This metauniverse will die. So will the universe in which you live. Neither should affect you unless you are a very, very, very slow reader. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies

title: Chapter 17: It’s All Crap!

text: “I’ve read what you gave me to read,” said the muse, after reading what I’d given her to read. “All 20,154 words, not including this chapter, of course. title: Chapter 19: Enjoy Life!
subtitle: Part X: Lessons From The Masters
text: “I’m really pissed,” I said to God. We were back in God’s Favorite Bar with a pitcher of beer. “What a waste! Do you know how much work I put into those characters? Do you have any idea how many pages I wrote and edited and rewrote and threw away? Do you know how many hours I spent working on those subplots? How many endings to the big scene? How many pages after that that don’t make any sense any more?” “Do you know how to spell omniscient?” Asked God. “Or course f ing I know. And I know you’re being a f ing idiot. You’re an idiot because you know what to do about this, and you’re not doing it. Think about it!” I thought. Waste? An imagined term. I was making the Third Classic Blunder. I wouldn’t know that was what it was called until I’d written The Third Classic Blunder, which now appears on page 101, but even now I could see it was a mistake. Pages, hours? Yes, I’d worked a lot, but writing is work that I enjoy. Why was I getting upset? I thought some more. I’d enjoyed it when I thought of what I’d been doing as writing. And I got angry about it when I thought of what I’d done as waste. Waste was imaginary. Once again, confusing imagina­ tion with reality. “Right,” said God. “And because you don’t know how to enjoy wasting things.” “How can I enjoy wasting things?” I asked. “You can enjoy anything,” God said. “That’s why I invented sentient beings after I invented life. Non-sentient beings just live. Which is fine. Sentient beings are able to enjoy life. Which is better. I wanted someone besides Me to enjoy life. Every minute of it.” “How can people enjoy life all the time?” I asked. “Some parts of life really suck.” “That’s bullsh ,” said God. “Death sucks. Life never does. There are only three reasons that people don’t enjoy every bit of their lives,” said God. One: they’re ignorant; two: they’re lazy; three: they’re idiots. “And what am I?” I asked? “Ignorant,,” God said. “You’re so ignorant you don’t even know where you are, or what you are. And you don’t know what’s around you. If you did, you’d find it easier to enjoy life.” “I know where I am,” I said. “No,” said God. “You imagine that you do. You probably think you’re in this chapter. But you’re not.” Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies

title: Chapter 2: What Is NaNoWriMo?
subtitle: Part II: The Metanovel
text: And suddenly my next chapter began. “Why am I writing this?” I asked myself. Of course, I knew the answer. It was a rhetorical question, another one of the literary devices I planned to use to improve the story and increase my word count. “It’s NaNoWriMo,” I answered myself. “I mentioned it in the last chapter.” “NaNoWriMo? What’s that?” I asked, pretending not to know and maintaining the illusion that this was a dialog, not a monolog. “NaNoWriMo is National Novel Writing Month,” I answered. “The idea is to write a 50,000 word novel during the month of November. The rules are pretty simple. Start after midnight November 1; finish before midnight November 30th. As far as NaNoWriMo is concerned, whatever you call a novel is a novel. Check out http://www.nanowrimo.org if you don’t believe me.” But the author believed what he had just said, and not just because it was November, and the author knew what he was writing, and not just because he was himself and knew what he was thinking, but because the chapter was now being narrated by another literary device. The author thought it was an omniscient narrator, a literary device that Wikipedia says: “could see and know everything that happens within the world of the story, including everything that all of the charac­ ters think and feel.” The Wikipedia was right, but the author was wrong. It was not an omni­ scient narrator. The narrator seemed omniscient because it could narrate what was in the author’s and other characters’ minds and because it could accurately narrate what would happen in the future of what the author thought would be a novel but which the narrator already knew would become a metanovel; for example, it knew that that on page 33 in the final draft, there will be a Chapter 5, which it knew will be called A Metanovel, in which the author will first decide that he is writing a metanovel; and because it knew that on Page 101, in a section called The Third Classic Blun­ der it will narrate how the author has made one of the classic blunders, the third one, in fact. Yet the narrator was not quite omniscient. It knows there will be a chapter called “The Not Quite Omniscient Narrator,” in which the narrator’s role in this metanovel will be narrated, but is not quite sure whether it will be chapter 10 or chapter 12, and is not quite sure whether it will appear on page 44, or 45, or 102. “I’m pleased to meet you,” said the author to the Not Quite Omniscient Narrator. The Not Quite Omniscient Narrator didn’t answer. Not that it couldn’t have answered. But as a matter of professional integrity it only narrated and never engaged in chit-chat. Right now it was narrating self-reflectively that it was wondering whether it would ever be­ come fully omniscient, and narrating that it was narrating that it was wondering. “Can we get back to NaNoWriMo?” The metanovel asked. “We need to keep this moving!” Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies Is That It? “Chapter 1 is about writing chapter 1. Chapter 2 is about why you are writing Chapters 1 and 2,” says my inner critic. Is that it? Are all the chapters going to be about writing chapters?” “I don’t know,” I say. “I’m still writing the first draft. I’ll let you know when I start editing.” “Please do,” says my inner critic, sarcastically. “I can hardly wait.” “No,” I report, as I start to edit. “There are going to be many different kinds of chapters. Some won’t be called chapters. And one will be about the worst day in my life.” “I remember that day,” says my inner critic. “You totally fucked up, didn’t you. Typical.” Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies

title: Chapter 20: Realize Where You Really Are
subtitle: Part X: Lessons From The Masters
text: “You’re in this chapter,”God said. “Very funny,” I said. “But I’m not in either chapter. I’m really sitting in my office. I’m alone,” I said. “Where is your office?” God asked. “In my house,” I said. “Where is your house,” God asked. “In Maine,” I said. “And where is Maine?” God asked. “This is getting a little silly,” I said. “Humor me while I show you how ignorant you are,” God said. “Okay,” I said. “Maine is in the United States. Which is in the North American continent. Which is on the planet Earth, which is in the Solar System, which is in the Milky Way galaxy, which is in the local cluster, which is in some universe, meta or not.” “Good,” said God. “Now relative to that whole big universe, where are you?” “I don’t understand?” I asked. “Where am I?” “Yes,” God said. “Supposing this was the space of the universe,” She flung her arms out and outlined an area. Where are you?” “I don’t quite know,” I said. “Then you don’t quite know where you are,” God said. “Not exactly,” I said. “But is that important?” “Vitally,” God said. “Why not take a guess? Just point our where you think you are?” “Alright,” I said. I thought for a moment. Earth was 93 million miles away from the center of the Solar System. The Solar System, I’d read once, was somewhere in the middle of one of the outer arms of the Milky way. I had no idea where the Milky way was relative to the local cluster. Or where that was relative to anything else. “I don’t know,” I said. “Take a guess,” God said. I pointed to a place in the space that God had made for the universe. It was about five feet across. I picked a spot about a foot from one of the edges. “I guess around here,” I said, pointing. “That’s what most people think when you ask them,” God said. “Somewhere out here. Here’s the truth. You are at the exact center of the universe.” God looked at me. “That’s a fact.” “Do you mean to tell me that the Solar System is at the center of the universe?” I asked. “It is,” said God. “But that’s not what I’m telling you. I’m telling that you are. “That’s illogical,” I said. “It’s egotistical. It’s improbable. Why should I be the one person who is at the center of the universe?” “Actually God is right,” said a man. He had a French accent. “I usually am,” God said. “She usually is,” the man agreed. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies “Who are you,” I asked. “I am Georges Lemaître,” he answered. “Monseigneur Georges Lemaître.” “Should I know you?” I asked. “You should,” said another man, “but most people don’t. Georges is the physicist who first hypothesized what we now call the Big Bang theory. Georges was a Catholic priest as well, but don’t hold that against him.” “And who are you,” I asked. “I am Arno Penzias,” the man answered. “And I’m Robert Wilson,” said another voice. “We’re here to explain why God says you are at the center of the universe.” Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies

title: Chapter 21: The Center of The Universe
subtitle: Part X: Lessons From The Masters
text: “I’m sorry,” I said. “But I don’t know who you are either.” “You’ve heard of the Big Bang, of course,” said Lemaître. “Yes,” I said. “I think most knowledgeable people have heard of it. “And does anyone who has read Prologue 2, And God Said: “Let There Be Light! Dammit!” Added the metanovel. “And you know about the cosmic background microwave radiation?” Lemaître asked. “Well, I know a little bit,” I answered. “I know that when you point a radio telescope to the sky you see the same radiation in every direction.” “That’s approximately correct,” said Lemaître. “We see a thermal black body spectrum at temperature 2.725 Kelvin, which peaks at the microwave frequency of 160.2 GHz, correspond­ ing to a 1.873 mm wavelength.” “I understand all of those words,” I said, “And I read the article you’re quoting in the Wiki­ pedia. But the importance is beyond me.” “That’s alright,” said Lemaître. “What’s important is that it’s a very faint glow which is the same in all directions.” “I understand that,” I said. “Penzias and Wilson discovered it,” Lemaître added. “They got a Nobel Prize for their work.” “I didn’t know that, either,” I said. “They did,” said Lemaître. “And it was important confirming evidence for the Big Bang. Do you understand why?” “No,” I said. “I knew there was a connection, but I’m not sure what it was.” Actually I did know the connection. The Wikipedia articles that I had read, research­ ing this chapter, had explained it. But dialog was better than a lecture would have been. “Both boring,” said my inner critic. “You remember that the further out in space an object is, the longer it must have taken for its photons to get to you?” Asked Penzias. “Yes,” I said. “So when you look far out in space you’re actually looking back in time.” “Yes,” I said. “And I remember that the red-shift tells us how far away an object is, so we know how long ago it emitted its light.” “That’s correct. The oldest confirmed galaxy, UDFj-39546284, is on the order of 13.2 billion light-years away—or 13.2 billion years in the past. More than billion years after the Big Bang. The background radiation is even older than that,” said Penzias. “The background radiation comes from the furthest detectable boundary of our uni­ verse,” said Wilson. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies “And since the boundary is the same in every direction, it follows that we cannot be nearer any part of the boundary than any other,” said Lemaître. I thought about that for a while. “That makes sense,” I said finally. “If the Big Bang Theory explains the origin of the universe, then the universe must have expanded from a point. So if you go back far enough in time, you must be at that point.” “Correct,” said Penzias. “And since this is true for every point in the universe, it means...” “It means that wherever you are you’re at the center of the universe,” I said. I thought about that for a moment. “It means that everyone is at the center of the uni­ verse.” I looked around me. I imagined perceiving the space in the room around me. I ima­ gined expanding my consciousness until I perceived—however dimly—the entire uni­ verse around me. And I was in the center. It was a great feeling. “Wow!” I said. “I am at the center! And so is everyone. That’s just incredible.” “If I may offer an opinion, both as a physicist, and as a Catholic priest,” said Mon­ seigneur Lemaître, “God is a fucking genius.” Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies

title: Chapter 22: I Know Where I Am!
subtitle: Part X: Lessons From The Masters
text: I looked around me in wonder. The world had changed. “Alright,” I said to God. “I know where I am. I’m at the center of the universe.” “That’s what I always told you, Michael,” said Mom. “Yes, Mom,” I said, “but you meant it figuratively, not literally. And you said I was the cen­ ter of Dad’s universe. God’s telling me that I am at the center of the universe. The whole uni­ verse. And so is everyone else.” “That’s right,” said God. “Now how can you not enjoy life when I’ve made you the center of all of creation?” “You might be taking some liberties with the physics,” I said to God, after I’d done some more research, “but damn! It feels good to stand here and feel the universe all around me.” “God can take all the liberties She wants to,” said my mother. “She’s God. That’s even better than being QFE.” “What’s QFE,” asked the metanovel. “It was my mother’s title before she died,” I answered. “Mom was Queen of Fucking Everything.” “Was then, am now,” said Mom. “I’m just DQFE.” I turned back to God. “It’s pretty cool,” I said. “It’s more than just cool,” God said. “Now that you know where you are, in the center of the universe, let’s work on understanding what you are.” “Alright,” I said. “In the next chapter,” God said. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies

title: Chapter 23: What Are You?
subtitle: Part X: Lessons From The Masters
text: “You said I didn’t know where I was,” I said to God. “I didn’t. Now I understand where I am. No matter what chapter I’m in, I’m always at the center of the universe.” “That makes you less ignorant than you were before,” said God. “But you still don’t know what you are. Knowing what you are will also make it easier to enjoy life. So what are you?” I thought for a while. “I’m a human,” I answered. “That’s your species,” said God, “But it’s not what you are.” “I’m a living thing,” I said. “That’s your category,” God said. “But it’s not what you are.” I thought for a while. God was getting at something. I knew She was. But I didn’t know, and I didn’t know what She was getting at. “I don’t know, and I don’t know what you’re getting at,” I said to God. “What am I?” “Think!” God said. “You are the same as all living beings. What are all living beings? From viruses to mammals?” Again I thought. I still couldn’t figure out what God was getting at. “Evolution,” said Charles Darwin. “Think about evolution." I thought again. What was evolution? I thought. It’s inheritance, variation, selection and it­ eration. I was originally a zygote. The zygote was the result of some blind sperm carrying a semi-random assortment of my Dad’s genes accidentally running head-first into an egg carrying a semi-random assortment of my Mom’s genes. I inherited from my Dad and Mom, and there was variation due to the largely accidental selection of genes in the egg and the sperm that acci­ dentally that united with it. Sexual reproduction produced a lot of variation. That was just one of many reasons that sex was cool. We evolved from simpler, pre-sexual creatures. If they divided they’d both have the same genes. So where did the variation come in there? I thought back to what I had learned about bio­ logy. Transcription errors. Cosmic rays. Variation in simple creatures came from damaged genes and transcription errors. In sexual creatures there were three mechanisms at work: accidental re­ combination of genes, accidental changes to genes, and mistakes in replication. In asexual repro­ duction only two. Then I saw it. I saw it and I laughed. “I’m an accident,” I laughed. “That’s right,” said God. “I’m a mistake!” I said. “It’s evolution. Variation is either an accident or a mistake. Every evolutionary step is the result of one or more mistakes and accidents.” “That’s right,” God said. I hated making mistakes. Every time I made a mistake I got upset. “And you’re always making mistakes,” my inner critic. “Because you’re an idiot.” “No,” said God. “People make mistakes because I designed them to make mistakes. Mis­ takes help people. Without mistakes perople would be boring. Mistakes help people evolve and create new things. Mistakes underlie all art and human creation. Mistakes help creations evolve. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies “Since I’m a mistake,” I said to God, smiling, “I’m just a mistake making a mistake accord­ ing to the design of the universe.” “That’s about right,” said God. “It changes the way you look at things, doesn’t it?” “It makes things less serious,” I said to God, “but doesn’t it make life meaningless.” “One thing at a time,” God said. “We’ll talk about life’s meaning later. Right now I want you to understand how to enjoy life.” It would be easier to enjoy life knowing I was at the center of the universe. It would be easy to enjoy life when I didn’t take things so seriously—seeing myself as a mistake and an accident who sometimes had accidents and made mistakes. I looked around me in wonder. The world had changed again. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies

title: Chapter 24: What’s Around Me?
subtitle: Part X: Lessons From The Masters
text: “Alright,” I said to God. “I’m a mistake at the center of the universe.” I smiled at the image. I imagined spreading my attention out, out, out and back, back, back in time toward the ancient explosion that started it all. Every time I did it, it felt good. “You need to practice that,” said the metanovel. “I do,” I said. “You need to practice a lot,” said the metanovel. “I will,” I said. “Now that you know where you are and what you are,” said God, “to further help you enjoy life you need to correctly perceive what’s around you. What’s around you?”to helplessness “Well, there are walls and floors. My wife’s in her office working on her book. Outside the house is the Salt Pond and the woods. And there are the people who live in my town, and the people in my state. And all the people on Earth. And, there are animals and plants, of course. Just a lot of stuff.” “It’s not animals and plants and stuff, as you so eloquently put it,” said God. “You’re sur­ rounded by your family.” “Not exactly surrounded,” I said. “I’ve got a wife in Maine. Three kids and their families in Boston. My brother in Florida and his family, my sister in Washington and hers.” “Your family is much, much bigger than that,” said God. “Well, yes,” I said. “If you count second and third and fourth cousins it’s bigger. But so what?” “You’ve failed to realize the elegance of God’s design,” said Lemaître. “The Big Bang puts you and everyone at the center of the universe.” “Quite so,” said Darwin. “And evolution not only shows that you’re a mistake. It also sur­ rounds you and everyone with family.” God snapped Her fingers and something changed. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies

title: Chapter 25: The Tree Of Life
subtitle: Part X: Lessons From The Masters
text: The chapter changed, of course. But that was one small detail. The big change was my per­ ception of time. Like everyone else, I had spent my life stuck in a single moment of time at a time. The time at any time was called ‘the present.’ The times yet to come were called ‘the fu­ ture.’ And the times that I had already experienced ‘the past.’ Like everyone and everything else I was dragged, helpless, from past times through future times through the present moment. That’s why self-referential metanovel writing was such a good imagination-building tool. Writing a self-referential metanovel takes time. Self-referential metanovel writing doesn’t have to take any more time than writing Morning Pages, Julia Cameron style. It can replace Morning Pages, or it can complement them. What’s different is the structure. In self-referential metanovel writing you write the imagined story of yourself doing what you want to do. That’s what I was doing. That’s what I am doing. I imagine being the kind of person that I want to be. I imagine doing the things I want to do —which right now is writing this sentence. I imagine organizing my tasks. I imagine making a list. I imagine doing the items on my list and imagine checking them off. I imagined being interrupted, then getting back on track. Getting interrupted and being dis­ tracted was a deeply rooted habit. It would take a lot of practice to develop a new one. But I was practicing. Then I stopped writing, and did what I had been imagining. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies

title: Chapter 39: How To Practice
subtitle: Part XII: Metapractice
text: “You heard my talk,” said Barbara Baig. “You’ve got my book in your bookcase. True, it’s about writing practice, but it applies to any kind of practice.” “I know,” I said, embarrassed. “I didn’t realize it until now. It’s obvious.” “I told you,” said the doorknob. “Well, he did finally remember it,” said the metanovel. “That’s something, isn’t it.” “More blather,” said my inner critic. “Shut up!” Barbara said to my inner critic. She turned to me. “Remember what I said when you heard me talk at the Blue Hill Library,” she said. “It’s also in my book.” I pulled out my copy of Barbara’s How to Be a Writer and checked it: Everyone accepts that athletes and musicians learn their skills and keep them honed through practice...We accept that if someone is going to undertake a public performance —on an athletic field, or in a concert—she has to build her skills and prepare herself through practice. ...it’s almost impossible to learn skills under performance conditions; ...we’re too focused on the result... “You’re right,” I said. “And you also said that one of the problems with most practice is that it’s focused on the characteristics of the finished product, not the skills needed to produce it. “Precisely,” Barbara said. “So what are the skills you need?” I thought for a moment. What did I need to do to get the result that I wanted? I didn’t have trouble putting words on paper. I’d had enough practice. And I wasn’t having trouble editing any more. I had, in earlier sections of the book, but I’d had enough practice. I wasn’t good organizing and making plans, but I could do it. But once I had a plan, I was horrible at following through. I would get distracted. I would lose track of time. I would forget that I was trying to follow a plan. “You think that your distraction due to ADD,” Barbara said. “You think it’s a personality trait.” “More like character defect,” said my inner critic. “Didn’t I tell you to shut up?” Asked Barbara. “Now shut up!” She turned back to me. “There’s no such thing as a personality trait,” said Barbara. “And there’s no such thing as a character defect. They’re not real. They’re imaginary. Don’t make the Third Classic Blunder. What’s real is skill, lack of skill, and degree of skill. That’s all.” “I already know that practice is a skill,” I said. “What’s missing.” “It’s so obvious,” said the doorknob. “The doorknob is right,” Barbara Baig said. “Think about it.” I thought: Practicing was a skill, but it had component skills, I thought. Perhaps one or more of those skills is missing or weak. I thought some more: To develop a skill, I’ve got to organize my practice. It’s a complex skill, so I’ve got to identify its components. I’ve got to organize time for my practice. And I’ve got to monitor my practice to ensure that it gets done. I thought some more: If something’s wrong I’ve got to take corrective action. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies I thought more. I’m a practiced thinker, I thought, so I have no trouble thinking. “I see what I need to do,” I said to Barbara. “I need to structure my practice.” The author was right, but he’d fail to structure his practice several times before he figured it out. subtitle: Part II: The Metanovel
text: How would the world react to his writing a self-referential metanovel? He didn’t care when he had started writing, but in what he thought would be the third-to-the-last draft but actually was the twentieth-to-the-last, he started to wonder. What do you do?” “I’m writing a self-referential metanovel,” he said. “It’s going to be called Self-referential metanovel Writing for D mmies: a self-referential metanovel.” “How very interesting,” she said. “Jim?” She tapped the shoulder of the man she was with. He turned from the conversation he’d been having. “Jim, this man is writing a self-referential metanovel.” “You’re writing a self-referential metanovel!” Jim said, surprised. “I am,” I said. “What a novel idea!” Jim said. text: If at first you don’t succeed, declare success. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies Epilogue 1:It’s Done! It’s done! Finally, my novel is done! I didn’t think I could do it, but I did. It was hard. In fact it was nearly impossible for me. The odds against it were enormous. But it was done. And I was a different person for having written it. Or I hope I will be. Once I finish writing it. Which won’t happen until I’ve started. Which is what I’m doing right now. Starting. I mean right now, while I’m writing this, not right now while I’m editing it. Or now while you’re reading it. The six paragraphs that you see at the top were in the first draft of the metanovel. They were among the first words I wrote. I haven’t edited them because they are historically significant, and for another reason that I’ve now forgotten. But one reason is enough. It’s true that I changed the number of asterisks. Originally there were ten, but when I edited the first draft I realized that ten was or were too many depending on dialect. But isn’t that what editing is for? I changed it to five. Five asterisks have held up through many subsequent edits, but I’m willing to change the number if someone makes a convincing argument. “You are an idiot,” said my inner critic. I ignored it. “Keep going,” said the metanovel. “Finish me.” Now I’m writing a draft version of this nearly complete paragraph. Or I had written it when I was writing the first draft. Now I’m editing it. And editing it again. And again. And now you’re reading it, of course. It’s not much. Or it wasn’t. But it’s a start! Or was. And I can’t hope to finish, which I still haven’t done—in this draft, anyway—unless I start. So I’m starting. Or I was starting, back when I started. “I think I’ve said this before,” said my inner critic, later, “but it deserves repeating: this is stupid.” I ignored it. “Keep going,” said the metanovel. I don’t have a plot, or characters, or a setting, or a theme. I don’t know what to call my nov­ el. Right now, as I’m writing this first draft, my working title is “The World’s Stupidest Novel.” It serves as a placeholder. I’ll change it when I know what I’m writing about. It also serves as a reminder of my deliberately low expectations. You might ask: why am I writing the epilogue first? Or rather, if you were asking it, you’d ask “Why are you writing the epilogue first.” If you had asked, which at this point I’m not saying you’ve done, I would have answered: “I have no idea what else to write. So I’m going to imagine success and declare victory. Why not?” Really, why not? Not knowing what this book will be about hasn’t stopped me from starting it. Not knowing what this sentence will be about hasn’t stopped me from starting it either. And not knowing won’t stop me from starting and then eventually finishing this sentence, as I am Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies confident that I will, sooner or later, even though it’s a convoluted self-referential sentence, and full of subordinate clauses, like that one, and these others, and this one. text: If at first you don’t succeed, whatever. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies Mom “Michael! Darling! You look wonderful!” Her Brooklyn accent and eighty years of heavy ci­ garette smoking made her voice unmistakable. “Mom!” I said, surprised. “What are you doing in my metanovel? You’re supposed to be dead.” “Dead, shmed,” she said. “If you think a little death can stop me, you’ve got another think coming. Can I smoke here?” “I guess so,” I said. We’d made her smoke outside the house while she was alive, but it seemed stupid to make her smoke outside the metanovel. And what was outside a metanovel? She reached into her battered purse, rummaged around and pulled out a pack of Camels and a Bic lighter. She pulled out a cigarette—her hands were still shaking, death hadn’t helped the tremor—and handed me the lighter. I lit her cigarette. She took a healthy drag. “Dad says hello,” she said and she blew out the smoke. “He’s playing bridge. Maybe he’ll come by later.” She looked around. “Page 53!” She said. “Very nice! I always knew you’d write a book some day. It’s really too bad you didn’t write it while Dad was alive.” “I’ve written a lot more than 53 pages,” I said. “They come later. And you’ll be in it later. In fact,” I checked the last draft, “the last page is 216.” “Wonderful, darling, wonderful.” She looked around. “Can I smoke here?” “You’re already smoking,” I said. “Let me get you an ashtray.” Her ashes were dropping on the page. “One nice thing about being dead,” she said. “you I don’t have to worry about cancer,” she laughed and took another drag. Led by our fearless Mom, we learned to laugh at death and adversity. After Dad died, my brother, Mark, and I wrote his obituary. Dad’s mother had emigrated to America from Hungary after she’d been forced into marriage. She had not bothered to divorce her husband before mar­ rying Dad’s father which made Dad technically illegitimate. Dad had been a preemie, not expec­ ted to survive, so his birth wasn’t registered for six months. As a result Dad had two birthdays a year—one on the day of his birth, the other the day of his registration. Dad died at age 84 and the headline we would use for the obituary that Mark and I wrote was obvious to us: Bastard Dies After 168th Birthday. Mom thought it was great. “So did I,” said Dad. “I’m dummy on this hand, so I thought I’d say hello.” “Hello,” I said. “Sorry, I can’t stay long,” said Dad. “My partner just laid down the rest of his hand. I’ve got to deal. Bye.” “Bye,” I said. “Bye,” Mom said. “Do you know how much money those crooks at the funeral home want for an urn?” Mom had asked as we were preparing for Dad’s memorial service. “Two hundred fifty dollars! It’s a jar, for God’s sake! We’re going shopping!” For twelve dollars we got a nice cookie jar where Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies most of Dad still rests, and for a few bucks each got small ceramic containers for each of us to have a bit of Dad. “Have you ever met my father?” I’d ask people. “No,” they’d say. I’d pull out Dad and make introductions. “Don’t listen to anyone who says your book is crap,” said Mom. “If you wrote it, I’m sure it’s wonderful.” Nothing stopped Mom. She’d talk to anyone she wanted to, make friends with anyone she wanted to, and fight anyone she had to. She’d work her way around bureaucracies by charm if possible, and by intimidation if charm didn’t work. She was street smart and intellectually curi­ ous, but a poor student. “The only way I got through high school,” she told us, “was by dating my teachers.” I wasn’t my mothers’ son. I was bookish and shy. Talking to strangers was an ordeal. And watching Mom in action was embarrassing. I just wanted to be left alone to read and dream. “Darling, you look wonderful!” Mom said again. “Can I smoke here?” “Yes, Mom,” I said. “Of course.” Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies Your Mother? “What’s your mother doing in your metanovel?” Asked my inner critic nastily. “She’s dead.” “

I walk out on the board. It’s shaking beneath me. I walk slowly. My friends below are shout­ ing. I walk near the end. I look over. I’ve got bad work habits; that makes me disorganized. I have no self-discipline; that makes me weak-minded. I’ll never finish writing it. If I finish writing it, I’ll never finish editing it. If I finish editing it, it won’t be very good. Together those mean that my metanovel is a hopeless effort. And my feet smell awful.” The Not Quite Omniscient Narrator saw that the author had fallen victim to one of the Three Classic Blunders. He hadn’t gotten involved in a land war in Asia, the First Classic Blunder; he hadn’t gone against a Sicilian when death was on the line, the Second. It was one more case of the author confusing what was real with what was imagined. Uncharacteristically he did something that wasn’t stupid. He could use his imagination and imagine understanding. And he did. The Pythagorean equation: a2 + b2 = c2 has many integer solutions. Fermat’s Theorem: no three positive integers can satisfy the equation an + bn = cn for n greater than two. The world’s mathematical minds had individually spent years and collectively spent centur­ ies of effort trying to prove the Theorem was true or finding a counterexample. Wiles produced a 400 page proof after six years of intense practice. He would master a branch of mathematics by reading the literature, working through the theorems, and then by practice. Practice! He’d practice, and practice, and practice, until solving problems in that branch of mathematics was as effortless as adding single digits is to most of us. Then he’d go on to the next branch, practicing, and prac­ ticing, and practicing it until he mastered it. text: If at last you find success, clean up the loose ends and you’re done. Self-Referential Metanovel Writing for D mmies Done At Last! Almost. My metanovel was finished. “Then why are you writing this?” Asked my inner critic. “You just said it was finished.” “I am,” I said, “But I learned something really important while I was editing it, and I don’t want to forget what I learned. I learned the importance of decision, imagination, belief, and prac­ tice. “And I learned the importance of having a safe place, and en-joying my life.” “Didn’t you write it in the first draft?” Asked my inner critic. “I did,” I said. “Except for the safe place part. That part was really important.” “And didn’t you write about it more in the fifth, and the twenty-third, and...” my inner critic listed the drafts during which I’d elaborated on the importance of decision, imagination, belief, and practice.” “Yes,” I said. “Except for the safe place part.” “Then why on earth are you writing it again?” My inner critic asked. “Are you an idiot?” “There’s a reason,” I answered. “If I keep writing, I’ll know what it is.” I thought back to November, writing my first draft. Almost all of the ideas that are in this fi­ nal version were in the first draft. But they were buried and disorganized. And they were in my head even before the first draft. Buried and disorganized. I knew them, but I didn’t understand them. “I didn’t practice,” I said. “I knew I should practice but I didn’t do it. Really I didn’t know how to. What I said about metapractice was true.” I thought back to November again. Writing the first draft hadn’t been hard. It took a little time, and it took almost no practice. And it was fun. I found that I cared about what I had writ­ ten. But I couldn’t finish it. I didn’t know how to finish it. I didn’t even know how to edit it. I’d edit the first five pages, or the first ten, and then quit. I’d try again. And then I’d give up. I’d get frustrated and put it away for weeks. I’d write new beginnings, and edit them. I’d get frustrated again. I’d get upset. I’d get angry. I’d get depressed. And finally, I started to practice. Really practice. I forced myself to do a complete editing pass, from the front to the back. I threw things out. I added things. But most of all, I read what I’d written. I paid attention. And I did what I’d been telling myself to do. “If you hadn’t been such a moron, you would have done it sooner,” said my inner critic. “Maybe,” I said. “But in the end I didn’t give up. That’s important to remember, too.” I did another complete editing pass. And read what I’d written. And applied some more. I kept doing it. Practice, Practice Practice! Then my metanovel came to life. It wanted to be finished. And then I really started to practice. I wrote and edited every day.
